chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
That which is in the body and consists of two, for one of them is half the wergild, like the two hands and the two eyes.

He (the narrator) said: So I said, 'A man whose eye was blinded?' He said: 'Half the wergild.' I said, 'So a man whose hand was cut off?' He said: 'Regarding it is half the wergild.' I said, 'So a man, one of his testicles is lost?' He said: 'If it was the left one, then for it is the (complete) wergild.' I said, 'And why? Did you not say, 'That which is in the body and consists of two, for each one is half the wergild?' He said: 'Because the offspring comes from the left testicle.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on blood money for the loss of one testicle in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between simple bilateral symmetry and functional asymmetry in determining blood money (diyah). While most paired organs like hands and eyes warrant only half the wergild for unilateral injury, the left testicle is an exception, commanding the full wergild due to its superior role in procreation according to contemporary medical understanding. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly method of integrating practical biological observations with legal principles to ensure equitable compensation.
